analytic.title: Host of haematophagous leeches

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The development of an efficient and cost-effective method for monitoring animal populations or biodiversity is urgently needed, and invertebrate-derived DNA (iDNA) may offer a promising tool for assessing the diversity and other ecological information of vertebrates. We studied the host species of a haematophagous leech (Haemadipsa japonica) in Yakushima by genetic barcoding and compared the results with those for mammal composition revealed by camera trapping. We analyzed 119 samples using two sets of primers by Sanger sequencing and one set of primer by next generation sequencing. The proportion of the samples that were successfully sequenced and identified to at least one species was 11.8-24.3%, depending on the three different methods. In all of these three methods, most of the samples were identified as sika deer (18/20, 6/15, 16/29) or human (2/20, 7/15, 21/29). The non-human mammal host species composition was significantly different from that estimated by camera trapping. Sika deer was the main host, which may be related with their high abundance, large body size and terrestriality. Ten samples included DNA derived from multiple species of vertebrates. This may be due to the contamination of human DNA, but we also found DNA from deer, Japanese macaque and a frog in the same samples, suggesting the mixture of the two meals in the gut of the leech. Using Haemadipsa japonica-derived iDNA would not be suitable to make an inventory of species, but it may be useful to collect genetic information on the targeted species, due to their high host selectivity.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The development of an efficient and cost-effective method for monitoring animal populations or biodiversity is crucial for rapid decision-making in conservation and management of wildlife. Traditional detection-based monitoring is time-consuming and labor-intensive (Whitesides et al. 1988;Hanya et al. 2003), and the precision of identifying species or age-sex classes may depend on the ability of the observers. Methods based on animal traces, such as feces, nests, or footprints, enable researchers to collect more data per unit effort than detection-based methods (Delibes et al. 2012;Hanya et al. 2017;Kanamori et al. 2017). However, one can only obtain limited information on the individual animal that left the trace compared with direct observation (Hanya et al. 2017). Camera trapping is a powerful method that can reveal not only the species or age-sex classes but also the behavior of the filmed animals (Pebsworth and LaFleur 2014), and it requires minimum effort in the field. However, the ability to identify age-sex classes also depends on the observers' abilities with detection-based surveys. In addition, camera trapping can be time-consuming with respect to the duration of setting cameras in the study site as well as the time needed for analysis.

Environmental DNA, or eDNA, is an emerging and promising monitoring tool for the study of biodiversity (Taberlet et al. 2012;Ficetola et al. 2016). Organisms leave their tissues in their environment (water, soil, etc.), and researchers can collect the organisms' deposited DNA by collecting samples of the environment. This can be used to ascertain the presence of a particular species by PCR amplification using species-specific primers (Fukumoto et al. Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 5 2015) or to make an inventory of species by sequencing barcoding regions with universal primers of the taxon using a next-generation sequencer (Ishige et al. 2017;Sato et al. 2017). eDNA is mostly used for aquatic ecosystems, as the substrate (water) can stir the deposited DNA through the environment.

As a monitoring tool for vertebrates, much attention has recently been paid to invertebrate-derived DNA, or iDNA. The idea is to sample the invertebrates that collect vertebrates' DNA. Target invertebrates are those animals that eat the feces, blood or carrion of vertebrates, such as leeches, mosquitoes, carrion flies and blowflies (Calvignac-Spencer et al. 2013a). Calvignac-Spencer et al. (2013a) argued that iDNA can potentially be used for studies on species biodiversity, genetic information of a targeted species (e.g.

genotyping and sexing), and disease transmission. Various species of invertebrates collect vertebrate DNA in a variety of ways, and each species selects vertebrate species in its own way. Therefore, we need to examine which invertebrates are appropriate for use in obtaining certain kinds of ecological information on vertebrates.

Aside from studies using haematophagous invertebrates (Kocher et al. 2017) and flies (Hoffmann et al., 2016;Hoffmann et al. 2017) to study diseases across landscapes and using flies to study diseases within primate social groups (Gogarten et al., 2019), iDNA has mostly been used to study the presence of a particular species or biodiversity (Schnell et al. 2012;Calvignac-Spencer et al. 2013b;Schubert et al. 2015;Lee et al. 2016;Perez-Flores et al. 2016;Rodgers et al. 2017;Schnell et al. 2018;Tessler et al. 2018;Axtner et al. 2019;Drinkwater et al. 2019). For example, Schnell et al. (2012) To confirm the effectiveness of iDNA, one needs to study the vertebrate community both by iDNA and conventional methods, such as transect census or camera trapping, and compare the results. Such studies have been conducted
for flies (Lee et al. 2016;Rodgers et al. 2017) and leeches (Weiskopf et al. 2018).

These studies reveal that iDNA collection from flies or leeches for a few weeks could detect more species of mammals than could a line transect census or camera trapping conducted concurrently. However, iDNA missed some of the very abundant species in the habitat. These results indicate that iDNA is an imperfect yet cost-effective method for making an inventory of mammals.

Most of the previous studies on iDNA were conducted in species-rich ecosystems, which is appropriate for testing its validity as a tool of monitoring biodiversity. One of the unexplored factors that need to be examined to confirm the validity of this method is the feeding preferences of the invertebrates, which would bias the kinds of species detected by this method (Schnell et al. 2015;Schnell et al. 2018) Compared with flying animals, they have advantages as a source of iDNA because they offer more DNA, and show high spatial resolution due to their lower movement ability (Schnell et al. 2015).

The purpose of this study is to reveal the host species of terrestrial heamotaphagous leeches (Haemadipsa japonica) by genetic barcoding in the coniferous forest of Yakushima, southern Japan, which has a simplified set of mammal fauna. Two previous studies on the host of this species have been conducted (Sasaki et al. 2005;Sasaki and Tani 2008) in northern and central

Japan, but it remains unanswered whether the leech positively selects the host species or they opportunistically feed upon the mammals they encounter. If the proportion of mammal species revealed to be fed upon by the leeches was similar to that of the relative abundance of each mammal species, then, we could conclude that the iDNA from leeches provides a promising monitoring tool for knowing the relative abundance of each mammal species. On the other hand, if the leeches are highly selective, they could be used as a tool for collecting the genetic information of a particular species. In order to understand how the choice of different sets of primers affects the results, we analyzed the mixture of DNA from the leech and tissues of mammals of known concentration for two sets of primers. We also analyzed samples by both Sanger sequencing and NGS to examine the possibility of 'mixing' DNA from two or more different species, either naturally or through contamination.

div.head: Study site
div.p: Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 9

This study was conducted in the coniferous forest of Yakushima, which is an island in the southwestern part of Japan (30°N, 131°E). We selected a study site in the western part of Yakushima with an altitude of 700-1300 m above sea level.

The dominant species include warm-temperate evergreen broad-leaved trees, such as Quercus acuta, Q. salicina, Distylium racemosum, and conifers, such as Cryptomeria japonica, Abies firma, and Tsuga sieboldii. Haemadipsa japonica is the only known haemadipsid leech in Yakushima (Tani and Ishikawa 2005).

div.head: Collection of leeches
div.p: We collected leeches during a census of Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) (Hanya et al. 2003;Hanya et al. 2005) conducted in August 2016, 2017 and 2018, with the aid of volunteers. We set a 7.5 km 2 census area and divided it into 30 500 m * 500 m quadrats. We positioned one point observer at an observation point in each quadrat. The point observer stayed at the observation point from ca 6:00-7:00 to 16:00 and collected leeches while wearing a mask and gloves. The collected leeches were kept in a 1.5 mL tube filled with 1 mL of 99% ethanol at room temperature. We did not collect leeches that touched the skin of the observers to avoid contamination by human DNA. This was repeated 5-7 days at each point. We collected leeches at 25 out of the 30 observation points.

div.head: Camera trapping
div.p: We set 30 camera traps (Trophy Cam HD ® Bushnell, Model119436) in the study We examined how the concentration of mammal-derived DNA affected the success of the PCR amplification by mixing DNA extracted from the tissues of leeches and mammals at various ratios. We measured the concentration of DNA in the solution extracted from the entire body of the H. japonica (in which it has been confirmed that mammal DNA was not amplified for any of the primer sets), blood of a wild Japanese macaque captured in Yakushima, commercially sold meat of a wild sika deer in Hokkaido (Cervus nippon yesoensis), and a finger of a wild small Japanese field mouse (Apodemus argenteus) captured in Inabu Field, Graduate School of Bioagricultural Sciences, Nagoya University, central Japan. Then, we diluted the solutions to 5.0 ng/μl and mixed mammal and leech DNA at ratios of 1:0 (positive control), 1:1, 1:10, 1:100, 1:1,000, 1:10,000, and 1:100,000. Next, we conducted PCR with the above two primer sets under the same conditions. We visualized the PCR products by electrophoresis. This was repeated five times for each mammal for each primer set.

div.head: Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 13
div.p: Massively-parallel sequencing using MiSeq

For the primer set SCPH02500/SCPL02981, we also performed massively -parallel sequencing of samples using one of the next-generation sequencing (NGS) machines, MiSeq. PCR condition was slightly changed from Sanger sequencing: the first denaturation at 94 °C for 10 min, 45 thermal cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 10 sec, annealing at 51 °C for 30 sec, and extension at 72 °C for 1 min, followed by the final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. PCR amplifications were prepared in a 25-μl volume containing 1 μl of template DNA, 2.5 μl of 10xEx Taq buffer, 0.5 μl of each 2.5 mM dNTP, 0.5 μl of each 10 μM primer, 0.2 μl of ExTaq polymerase (Takara Bio Inc.) and 18.3μl of dH2O.

Negative controls were included in the PCR, and we confirmed that it was not amplified. We chose this condition and this primer set because we could amplify more samples under this condition than that used for Sanger sequencing and also more than the primer set 16Smam1_out-F/16Smam2_out-R/16Smam1_out_blkhum. However, another shorter region was also amplified, since there were two bands for some samples

div.head: Sequence data analysis
div.p: For the sequences obtained by Sanger sequencing, we assigned the identity of the obtained sequences through an online BLAST search (Basic Local Assignment Search Tool; https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) on November 5, 2018. We used the 'Nucleotide collection (nr/nt)' option for the database. We chose the species that showed the highest identity but rejected them when the maximum identity was less than 98%. All of the samples showed similarity to the Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 15
sequence of the species distributed in Yakushima.

For the NGS data, to identify the species for each read, we first made a local database for the animal species known to be distributed in Yakushima (Table 1). They were 13 species of mammals native to Yakushima, three introduced mammal species, human, and one native frog species (Rana tagoi yakushimensis). The frog was included because it was detected by Sanger sequencing. For the two species of field mice (A. speciosus and A. argenteus), the sequence was not available in the database, so we newly sequenced the region and added to the database using the tissue samples collected in Inabu.
Then, each read was queried to the database using the command blastn (NCBI).

We discarded reads with <98% maximum identity or when the length of the matched sequence was less than 200 bp. Under this criterion, among the 12,038,444 reads, no similarity with the vertebrate database was found for 11,573,147 reads. When the number of reads for the sample identified as the vertebrate species was less than 100, we did not include the reads for further analysis because sample misidentification is inevitable on the Miseq platform (Kircher et al. 2012) (Supplemental Material 1). None of the remaining 465,297 reads showed maximum identity >98% for two or more species.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Even though we found that mammals were not the only host for leeches, we had no data on the relative abundance of humans and frogs in the study site.

Therefore, we compared the relative abundance of only non-human mammals detected by camera traps and genetic analysis of the leeches. We tested whether the proportion in the number of the host mammal species estimated by Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 16

genetic analysis differed significantly from the expected number of detections calculated based on the relative abundance of each mammal species, which was estimated by camera trapping. For the results of host identification, we examined the following three cases: primer set 16Smam1_out-F/16Smam2_out-R/16Smam1_out_blkhum (16Smam, hereafter) (Sanger sequence), SCPH02500/SCPL02981 (SCPH, hereafter) (Sanger sequence), and SCPH02500/SCPL02981 (NGS). Raw numbers of filmed animals may bias the estimates of abundance for each species. First, movies filmed at short intervals might capture the same individuals repeatedly and thus over-estimate its abundance. To avoid such bias, we can discard additional movies taken within a short interval (e.g. 30 min). However, for group-living animals, such as Japanese macaques, repeated filming may reflect a larger group size, and thus the crude number of filming events may be a better index.

Second, more than one individual can be filmed in a single movie. Third, even though the frequency of filming events may reflect the encounter rate for the leech with the animal species, it does not account for the biomass of the species.

Considering all of these possibilities, we examined the following four parameters as indices of animal abundance: (1) crude number of filming events, (2) number of filming events after discarding other movies taken within 30 minutes, (3) average number of individuals filmed in one movie x (2), (4) body mass of the species x (3). Data on body size were taken from Agetsuma et al. (2011) for sika deer (Cervus nippon yakushimae), from Mori (1979) for Japanese macaques and Ohdachi et al. (2009) for other species. See Supplemental Material 3 for detail. The expected number of samples was less than five for most of the mammals. To make expected the numbers more than five, we combined all of Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 17

the non-deer mammals and compared this amalgam with deer, the most common species. We compared the observed (by iDNA) and expected (from camera trapping) number of samples between the sika deer and the other non-human mammals using the χ 2 test by R 3.2.2 (R_Core_Team 2015).

GH, KM, TK, NSH, and TH conducted genetic analysis, GH, YO SH, TH, HO, and YH set and maintained the camera traps, GH, YO, TH, MH, YK, YK, SJ, AO, IS, TT, and HY collected the leeches, HS and HK collected the mice specimen, GH and YK collected the macaque specimen, and GH, KM, and TN dissected the leeches.

div.head: Results
div.p: The experiment on mixing mammal and leech DNA indicated that the threshold DNA concentration below which the mammal DNA could not be detected was different between the primer sets and also by the mammal species (Fig. 1, Table 2). It was possible to detect mammals with a lower concentration of mammal DNA using the primer set 16Smam than using the primer set SCPH. Sika deer was detected at a lower concentration than Japanese macaques and mice in the primer set 16Smam, but opposite was true for the primer set SCPH.

For the primer set 16Smam, 20 out of 119 samples (16.8%) were successfully sequenced and identified to one species. For the primer set SCPH, it was 15 samples (12.6%). For the NGS using primer set SCPH, 29 samples (24.3%) included at least 100 reads for the sample that was successfully identified as vertebrate species. Forty-four samples showed positive results for at least one of the three methods. Among them, seven samples showed positive Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 18 results for all of the three methods, seven for two methods, and the remaining 30 samples showed positive results by only one method (Supplemental Materials 2).
There was no case in which the results of different methods were contradictory to each other.
Most of the sequences were identified as sika deer or human. For the primer set 16Smam, 18 samples were identified as sika deer and two as human.

For the primer set SCPH, seven were identified as human, six as sika deer, one as frog (R. tagoi), and one as raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides). For the NGS using primer set SCPH, 16 samples included reads identified as sika deer, 21 samples for human, two samples as Japanese macaque, and two samples for the frog. For ten samples, more than one species were identified per sample, even when infrequent reads were excluded. Deer and human were detected for eight samples, frog, human and deer were detected for one sample, and deer, macaque and frog were detected for one sample.
Camera traps functioned for 8658 camera-days in total. We obtained 2542 videos of sika deer, 636 of Japanese macaques, 653 of field mice, 22 of Japanese weasels, and 14 of feral dogs.

The proportion of the non-human mammal host species of the leeches was significantly different from the relative abundance calculated from the camera trap data (Table 2). The proportion of the host species (deer vs non-deer) was significantly different from the abundance of the mammals when we calculated the expected values based on the crude number of filming events, the number of filming events after discarding repeatedly filmed animals, or the number of filming events multiplied by the mean number of filmed individuals.
This tendency was statistically significant for 16Smam (Sanger sequence) and Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 19

NGS but not for SCPH (Sanger sequence), due to the small number of samples identified as non-human mammals. When we took body mass into consideration, however, we could not reject the null hypothesis that leeches feed upon mammals based on their relative biomass.

div.head: Host selection by Haemadipsa japonica in Yakushima
div.p: We found that the composition of mammal species revealed by camera trapping and the host species of the leech Haemadipsa japonica differed. Sika deer was more frequently identified as hosts of the leech than expected by their detection rates by the camera traps. Field mice were not detected and Japanese macaques were only infrequently detected from the leeches, even though their detection rates by camera trapping were not so low. However, when the large body size of a sika deer was considered, we could not reject the null hypothesis that the leeches feed on deer more often than on other species due to their highest relative biomass among the mammals here.

The fact that the sika deer was the major host of leeches in Yakushima may be related to the large abundance, body mass and terrestriality of the deer, and the effects of these factors were considered in the statistical analysis. The probability of encountering the leeches is expected to be the highest for the most abundant species. Respiratory CO2 is one of the suggested cues that leeches use to detect mammals (Yoshiba 1996), and large-bodied animals are likely to emit more such cues. Terrestrial animals would offer more opportunity for leeches to attack than partially arboreal field mice or Japanese macaques (Hanya et al. 2007;Sakamoto et al. 2012). The (partial) arboreality of mice and Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 20

macaques was already reflected in their detection rates by the cameras, since the cameras were set near the ground. High grooming capability of Japanese macaques may also related with the low detection rate of this species in leeches.

The main target of grooming by this species is the eggs of louse, each of which is only 0.6 mm in length (Tanaka and Takefushi 1993). Considering the high dexterity of their fingers, it would be easy for them to remove leeches from their skin. Actually, researchers in Yakushima observed two cases of Japanese macaques removing a leech from their own or their infant's body in the lowland of Yakushima (Yosuke Kurihara and Mari Nishikawa, unpublished data). The grooming done by deer functions to remove ticks (Heine et al. 2017), but because they use their mouth for grooming, their manipulation ability would be lower than that of macaques. The difference in hair length and the major posture taken on the ground may also affect the accessibility for leeches. Further research based on the behavioral observation of both leeches and host animals would be interesting to explore the reason on the host preference by the leeches.

div.head: Comparisons between the results of NGS and Sanger sequencing
div.p: Even though the main conclusion, i.e., that sika deer is the major host for this leech, was the same among the three different methods, the results were not always the same when examining this for each sample. Concerning the mismatches of the two Sanger sequencing methods, the main reason would be the blocking primer of human sequence and the lower sensitivity of SCPH than 16Smam, as shown by the mixing experiment. In addition, the primer set 16Smam may not be able to detect the frog sequence (#293).

div.head: Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 21
div.p: There were 15 cases in which we detected the host by NGS but not by Sanger sequencing. When human DNA is dominant in the sample, amplification is blocked by the primer set 16Smam but not by the primer set SPCH in NGS (possibly in the cases of #210, 229, 230, 233, 235, 236, 237, 246, 250, 252, 268).
Alternatively, when the DNA of multiple species of non-human vertebrates are mixed, Sanger sequencing is likely to be inhibited (#226, 271).

There were also instance of the opposite case (N=15) in which hosts were detected by Sanger sequencing but not by NGS. The reason for this remains unknown, but it might be related to the reads that could not be assigned to any vertebrate sequences. These would probably result from the shorter fragments obtained in the 1 st PCR of NGS (see methods). Shorter fragments are easier to bind flow cells than longer ones, which might have prevented the detection of vertebrate-derived DNA in NGS. Unfortunately, in our system, we fail to find a primer set and optimal PCR conditions that can amplify only one region of a short fragment length. We can expect shorter fragments to lower the rate of sequencing error and improve amplification success (Axtner et al. 2019). In the future, thorough examinations of various primer sets will be necessary (Axtner et al. 2019). Yakushima, and they have never been handled in our laboratory, so it is also unlikely that the sample was contaminated by the frog DNA in the laboratory.

div.head: Detecting multiple host species from one individual of leech
div.p: Due to the small number of samples, it is difficult to conclude that DNA from both meals could have been detected. Further examination with many more samples, or a feeding experiment on multiple species by captive leeches, is required.

div.head: Potential bias
div.p: We need to examine whether any biases lowered the probability of detection of a particular species, both for camera trapping and genetic analysis. Sollmann et al. (2013) summarized the problems of regarding detection rates of different species in camera trapping as an index of the relative abundance of each species. For example, partially arboreal species and species with smaller home ranges are less represented than expected from their relative abundance. Large species are more likely to be filmed more often because the sensor of the camera can detect larger animals more easily. In Yakushima, all of these factors would bias results toward higher detection of the largest and terrestrial sika deer. Therefore, the proportion of sika deer in our camera trapping may have been an overestimation of the relative abundance of deer.
Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 23

However, we found that, in spite of this potential bias, the species composition of the hosts of leeches was even more biased toward deer. Therefore, our conclusion of the selective feeding upon deer by leeches remains unchanged, even considering the bias regarding camera trapping.

The sequence of a particular species may not be amplified with the sets of primers used in this study. We need to examine this possibility in particular for macaques, because we used blocking primer for human sequence was included in the primer set 16Smam. We designed the blocking primer so that the sequences were different between the macaque and human for the corresponding sequence with the blocking primer (Table 1). According to the mixing experiment of leech and mammal DNA, we confirmed that macaque DNA can be amplified even with blocking primer of human sequence. The experiment also showed that the DNA of Japanese macaques may likely be amplified less than that of sika deer using the primer set 16Smam but more than that of deer using the primer set SCPH (Fig. 1). However, underrepresentation of Japanese macaques was consistent between the two primers, so we believe the result was robust. versicolor or Syrmaticus soemmerringii) for 5 samples (Sasaki et al. 2005). In Kanagawa, central Japan, hosts were identified as sika deer for 17 samples and wild boar (Sus scrofa) for 14 samples (Sasaki and Tani 2008). Artiodactyla is abundant in many forested landscapes in Japan (Saito and Koike 2013;Ikeda et al. 2016). They are all terrestrial and large-bodied and not as dexterous in the removal of external parasite as Japanese macaques (Ohdachi et al. 2009).

div.head: Hosts of
div.p: However, in Vietnam, the host species found for the congeneric unidentified leech was more diversified, including Artiodactyla (pig, serow, cow and muntjac), Lagomorpha (rabbit) and Carnivora (badger) (Schnell et al. 2012). In a study in Bangladesh, 12 species of non-human mammals were detected by Haemadipsa leech-derived iDNA, including Artiodactyla (cow, pig, and muntjac), Rodentia (mouse), Carnivora (dog and civet), Primates (macaque), and Scandentia (tree shrew). To reveal the reasons for the differences among these studies, it would be necessary to conduct studies similar to the present one that examine mammal communities both by leech-derived iDNA and conventional monitoring (e.g. camera trapping) in more species-rich ecosystems.

Our finding that primates were not fed upon by Haemadipsa leeches may not be a general tendency. In Bangladesh, the proportion of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) included in the hosts of leeches was more than that found by camera trapping (Weiskopf et al. 2018). It is difficult to examine the selectivity of the leeches in that study because the mammal diversity is much higher than in Yakushima. The feeding strategy of leeches can vary with the species even within the same genus (Gasiorek and Rozycka 2017), as well as with the behavior of the host animals, such as strata use (Reed and Bidner 2004). Much more study would be needed to generalize the findings on the Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 25
preferred and avoided host taxa of leeches.

The results found in Japan, including those of this study, suggest that the iDNA from Haemadipsa japonica is not appropriate for make an inventory of mammals, unless the sample size is very large. This species may be more suitable as a material to provide genetic information on a particular species of ungulates, such as sika deer or Japanese serow. In the future, we need to examine whether the iDNA could be used for genetic population monitoring, such as sex determination and individual identification. Data on the life history and behavior of leeches would also be needed to interpret the results, such as the time interval between feeding and sampling (Schnell et al. 2015). However, the studies in Vietnam, Bangladesh and Borneo indicated that the hosts were taxonomically variable (Schnell et al. 2012;Weiskopf et al. 2018;Axtner et al. 2019), so other Haemadipsa leeches might be suitable for making a species inventory.

In conclusion, Haemadipsa japonica showed strong bias for sika deer as a host over other mammals, compared with the relative abundance estimated by camera trapping. This leech species would be more suitable to collect genetic information for the deer, rather than making a species inventory in its habitat.

site. Cameras were set to record videos of 30 s and placed 50 m directly north or south from the observation points. We deployed cameras during the period of July 15-17, 2014, and retrieved them from June 28 to July 5, 2015. We changed Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 10 batteries and SD cards in August and December 2014 and in March 2015. Details of the camera settings are described in Hanya et al. (2018). Even though the period when we set cameras does not overlap with the period when we collected leeches, the abundance of sika deer and Japanese macaques did not change considerably between the two periods, according to the census of these animals (Hanya et al., unpublished). Sample processing and extraction of DNA In September 2018, among the 126 samples collected over the three years, 92 leeches were dissected, and their gut (crop and crop ceca) was removed and ground with a bead crusher (Bead Smash 12 BS-12 ® WAKENYAKU) for 15-120 s at 4200 rpm after evaporating the remaining ethanol. The 27 samples became completely dry due to the evaporation of the ethanol, so the entire body was ground. The remaining seven samples were discarded by mistake or because they were rotten. To avoid cross-contamination among samples, the scalpel and tweezers were wiped with ethanol and then flame-cleaned each time different samples were handled. The desk was also cleaned with ethanol each time different samples were analyzed. We extracted DNA using QIAamp DNA Mini Kit ® Qiagen following the manufacturer's protocol. Dissection and DNA extraction were conducted at a different workspace from the subsequent analysis. Sanger sequencing First, we tried the original set of primers (16Smam1 and 16Smam2) used in Calvignac-Spencer et al. (2013b); however, we always obtained multiple bands and thus it was impossible to find an optimal PCR condition to amplify only a Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 11 single region. Therefore, we used two different sets of primers for Sanger sequencing, both of which amplify the 16S rRNA regions of the mitochondrial genome. For the primers SCPH02500 (5'-TTACCAAAACATCACCTCT-3') and SCPL02981 (5'-ATCCAACATCGAGGTCGTAA-3') (Matsui et al. 2007) (fragment size ca 503 bp), we conducted PCR under the following conditions: an initial denaturation at 94°C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of 10 s at 94°C, 30 s at the annealing temperature of 51°C, 1 min at 72°C, and a final extension at 72°C for 10 min. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were performed in 15 µl reaction volumes containing 10-15 ng genomic DNA, 1 × PCR buffer, 0.2 mM of each dNTPs, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.2 µM of each primer and 0.5 U of GoTaq polymerase (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). PCR products were electrophoretically separated on a 2.0% agarose gel and visualized using ethidium bromide in 1× TAE; all products exhibiting a single DNA fragment were selected for sequencing. These selected products were then purified using ExoSAP-IT (Affymetrix, Cleveland, OH, USA). Direct sequencing of both sequence directions was conducted using an ABI PRISM BigDye Terminator version 3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems) on an ABI 3500 Genetic Analyzer. We also used a newly designed set of the following primers covering the region used in a fly-derived iDNA study (Calvignac-Spencer et al. 2013b): 16Smam1_out-F (5'-ATAAGACGAGAAGACCCTATGGAG-3'), and 16Smam2_out-R (5'-TGAACTCAGATCACGTAGGACTTT-3'), and blocking primer of human DNA 16Smam1_out_blkhum (5'-CCTATGGAGCTTTAATTTATTAATGCAAACAGT-spacerC3-3') (fragment size: ca 366 bp). The blocking primer was designed so that the amplification of only human DNA, but not other mammal DNA, was inhibited (Vestheim and Host of haematophagous leeches Hanya et al. 12 Jarman 2008). PCR amplifications were prepared in a 25-μl volume containing 1 μl of template DNA, 2.5 μl of 10xEx Taq buffer, 0.5 μl of each 2.5 mM dNTP, 0.5 μl of forward and reverse 10 μM primer, 10 μl of the blocking primer, 0.125 μl of ExTaq polymerase (Takara Bio Inc.), 0.1 μl of T4 gene 32 protein (Nippon Gene Co., Ltd.), and 8.275 μl of dH2O. Negative controls were included in the PCR and confirmed that it does not amplify. After confirming successful amplification by electrophoresis and purification by isopropanol precipitation, the PCR products were directly sequenced with a BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit and a 3130 Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA).

shorter band: ca 200 bp). For the NGS, we prioritized having more samples rather than having only one band. For the 53 samples that were successfully amplified, we purified the PCR products with Agencourt AMPure XP (Beckman Coulter). Following procedures of library preparation, sequencing on MiSeq, and bioinformatics were based onHayakawa et al. (2018). We conducted the second PCR to attach the specific dual indices and sequencing adapters with KAPA HiFi HS ReadyMix (Nippon Genetics Co Ltd.) and Nextera XT Index Kit (Illumina, Inc.) in a total volume of 25 μl mixture containing 2.5 μl each of forward and reverse primers, and 2.5 μl of purified first PCR solution, 12.5 μl of KAPA, and 5Host of haematophagous leechesHanya et al. 14μl of water with 5 thermal cycles. The DNA concentration of the purified 2 nd PCR products was measured by Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit, and the DNA solutions for all samples were pooled so that the estimated molarity from each sample was equal. We sequenced this library with other libraries unrelated to this study and 5% PhiX spike-in on an Illumina MiSeq using MiSeq Regent Kit v3 (600 cycles).The read lengths from the MiSeq run were 301 bp (forward sequences), 8 bp (forward indices), 8 bp (reverse indices), and 301 bp (reverse sequences). The MiSeq base calls were converted to FASTQ files using configureBclToFastq.pl implemented by the bcl2fastq conversion software v1.8.4 (Illumina) (options:no-eamss, mismatches 0, and use-bases-mask Y300n,Y8,Y8,Y300n). The FASTQ files were demultiplexed using clsplitseq in Claident v0.2.2016.04.07(Tanabe and Toju (2013); https://www.claident.org). Read pairs with low-quality index sequences were discarded, that is, where the index sequences included nucleotide(s) with a quality score < 30 (option: minqualtag = 30). Since quality scores of nucleotides in the reverse sequences were low in this run possibly due to low diversity of the library and batch effect, we used only the forward sequences.

There were ten cases in which multiple vertebrate species were detected from a single individual leech. Since we have excluded results that can arise by misidentification on the Miseq, this could either be because of contamination or mixture of the blood of the last and the one previous meal. For the majority of cases (eight), human DNA was detected, so the possibility of contamination Host of haematophagous leechesHanya et al. 22 during sampling, processing, extraction and amplification cannot be ruled out.However, since there were two cases in which DNA of deer, macaque and frog were simultaneously detected, we assume it is possible that the DNA of the last two or three meals were detected. These two samples (#226 and 271) were dissected by different persons at different desks, with the DNA extracted and amplified at different times, so it is unlikely that DNA was cross-contaminated from one sample to another.
